paragraphs: Strictly speaking, no government is simple. A lone ruler still needs subordinate magistrates, and a popular government still needs a head. So in the way executive power is shared out, there is always a gradation from the greater number to the lesser. The difference is that sometimes the many depend on the few, and sometimes the few on the many.

Sometimes the power is divided equally. This happens either when the parts depend on one another, as in the government of England, or when each part is independent of the others but its authority is incomplete, as in Poland. This last form is bad, because it gives the government no unity and leaves the State without a bond to hold it together.
Is a simple government or a mixed one better? Political writers argue over this question endlessly. It has to be answered the same way we answered the earlier question about all forms of government.

Simple government is better in itself, precisely because it is simple. But when the executive power does not depend enough on the legislative power — _i.e._ when the prince is more closely tied to the Sovereign than the people are to the prince — this imbalance must be corrected by dividing the government. For then all the parts have just as much authority over the subjects, while their division makes them, taken together, less strong against the Sovereign.

The same disadvantage can also be prevented by appointing intermediate magistrates. They leave the government whole, and serve only to balance the two powers and maintain their respective rights. The government is then not mixed but moderated.

The opposite problem can be cured in a similar way: when the government is too lax, tribunals can be set up to concentrate it. This is done in all democracies. In the first case the government is divided to make it weak, in the second to make it strong. The highest degrees of both strength and weakness are found in simple governments, while mixed forms give a middling strength.
